introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Points : 10 + (5 + 5 + 5) = 25, conformes au sujet. Points des sous-questions : a = 10, b = 15.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain the processes by which River Mungo in Cameroon erodes and transports its load.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**River Mungo** is a river of south-western Cameroon which rises in the **western highlands** near the Cameroon Volcanic Line (Mount Manengouba and Mount Kupe area), flows **south** across the volcanic and crystalline basement rocks and finally across the **coastal sedimentary lowland** to the Atlantic coast (Gulf of Guinea). It has a strong flow in the long rainy season. Its erosion and transport follow the general processes of a river; the details depend on the energy of the river along its course. (The route is given in general terms only.)

**A. Processes of erosion**

1. **Hydraulic action.** The force of the moving water alone presses on the banks and the bed, forces water and air into cracks, and **loosens and removes** rock and soil. It is strongest at floods, in rapids, at waterfalls and on the outside of meanders.
2. **Abrasion (corrasion).** The **load carried by the river** (sand, pebbles and boulders of basalt and granite) is scraped, hammered and rolled against the bed and banks, which **wears them down like sandpaper**. It forms **potholes** and deepens the channel in the upper course (**vertical erosion**).
3. **Attrition.** The pieces of load **knock against each other** and against the bed, and are broken and **rounded and reduced in size** downstream (large angular boulders in the upper course; small, rounded pebbles and sand in the lower course).
4. **Corrosion (solution).** Acid river water **dissolves** soluble minerals and rocks (limestone or calcite cement, and salts), and weathers the volcanic minerals chemically in this humid tropical climate.

**B. Processes of transport** (the load is carried in four ways)

1. **Solution.** Dissolved minerals (calcium, sodium, bicarbonate, silica) are carried in the water.
2. **Suspension.** Fine particles (clay and silt) are held up by the turbulence of the water. They make the river brown, especially at flood.
3. **Saltation.** Sand and fine gravel are **lifted and carried in short hops** along the bed.
4. **Traction.** The **largest pebbles, cobbles and boulders** are **rolled, dragged or pushed** along the bed (the bed load), moving only at flood.

**C. Controls and relation to the Mungo.** The **competence** (the largest particle that can be moved) and the **capacity** (the total load that can be carried) increase with velocity and discharge (the Hjulstrom relation: coarse particles need a high velocity to be eroded, but fine clay needs a fairly high velocity too, because it is cohesive). In the **steep upper course** the water flows fast over resistant volcanic and basement rock, so **vertical erosion (downcutting)** dominates (V-shaped valley, rapids, waterfalls, potholes) and the load is coarse and angular. In the **lower course**, in the coastal lowland, the gradient is small, the river **meanders**, lateral erosion undercuts the outer banks, and the load is fine (sand, silt, clay) and is carried in suspension and solution, and is **deposited** as bars, levees and a floodplain, and in the estuary. During floods in the rainy season erosion and transport are at their greatest.

(A labelled sketch of the long profile of the river, and of the four methods of transport, is credited.)

**(i) Piedmont environment (5 marks).** The piedmont is the foot of a mountain or fault scarp, where steep mountain streams drop their load on **alluvial fans** and **braided-stream** plains (a piedmont or fan environment).

- *Composition:* **coarse, immature sediment**: **conglomerates and breccias** (pebbles, cobbles and boulders of the mountain rocks), **arkose and poorly sorted sandstones** with a muddy matrix. Fragments are of **rock** and feldspar (lithic and feldspathic), so the composition is **immature**. Iron oxide gives them red colours in a hot climate.
- *Texture:* **very poorly sorted** (boulders to mud together), clasts **angular to sub-rounded** (short transport), **matrix-supported** (debris flow deposits) or clast-supported (stream deposits).
- *Structures:* **crude bedding**, lenses and channel fills, **imbrication** of pebbles, large-scale **cross-bedding**, a wedge shape thinning away from the mountain, normal or reverse **grading** in some beds, mud cracks on the finer layers, and **very few fossils**.

**(ii) Deep marine environment (5 marks).** Deep water below the wave base, on the continental slope, rise and the abyssal plain.

- *Composition:* **fine-grained rocks**: **shale, mudstone and marl**, **greywacke** (a dirty sandstone with a clay matrix, rock fragments and feldspar) deposited by **turbidity currents**; **calcareous oozes** (chalk and fine limestone made of the shells of foraminifera and coccoliths) above the carbonate compensation depth; **siliceous oozes** (radiolarian chert, diatomite) below it; abyssal red clay.
- *Texture:* very **fine**, **well-sorted** pelagic muds and oozes; the turbidites are **graded** and poorly sorted with a muddy matrix.
- *Structures:* **graded bedding** and **Bouma sequences** (graded base, parallel lamination, ripple cross-lamination, fine mud) in turbidites, **sole marks** (flute and groove casts), **convolute lamination and slump structures**, **thin regular lamination**, alternating sand and mud beds (rhythmites); no sign of wave action or of desiccation; the fossils are **planktonic** (foraminifera, radiolarians, graptolites or ammonites in old rocks) with little bottom life (the water is deep, dark and poor in oxygen).

**(iii) Transgressive shorelines (5 marks).** A transgression is the **advance of the sea over the land** when sea level rises or the land sinks, and the shoreline moves landwards.

- *Composition:* a **basal conglomerate or sandstone** (a **transgressive lag** of pebbles and shells) made of the weathered material of the old land surface, mostly **quartz**, with **quartz arenite** (mature) and **glauconite**; above it, **shales, then limestones** as the water becomes deeper.
- *Texture:* the shore sands are **well-sorted and well-rounded** (reworked by waves), the conglomerate has **rounded pebbles**; the sediment becomes **finer upwards**.
- *Structures:* a **fining-upward and deepening-upward sequence** (conglomerate, sandstone, shale, limestone), resting on an **unconformity** (erosion surface), **onlap** of the beds on the old land surface, **wave ripples and cross-bedding**, **burrows** and shelly beds, rich **marine fossils** and a continuous (**diachronous**, younger landwards) deposit that migrates inland.

(Each environment is credited for composition, texture and structure; a small sketch of each is useful.)
